poster.title: The Rabbits
poster.bookOrigin: Australian picture book written by John Marsden and illustrated by Shaun Tan; first published in 1998.
poster.creator: Shaun Tan
poster.alt: A vast pale projecting ship rises over angular marching rabbits with tall black hats; yellow clouds surround a dark sky opening with white title, above pale sloping ground and a gold medal.
poster.blurb: A towering ship and an angular procession turn arrival into an imposing spectacle.

notes.title: The displayed edition
notes.body: Hachette Australia hardback, 1 May 2008, ISBN 9780734410788. The picture book first appeared in 1998; the displayed publisher image is dated to the selected product.

notes.title: Writing and image-making
notes.body: John Marsden wrote the text and Shaun Tan made the illustrations. Tan’s creator page discusses the work’s colonisation context; Reading Australia records the original 1998 book.

notes.title: A visible design relationship
notes.body: The projecting hull and pointed hats repeat an angular rhythm. Dark ground strokes reinforce the slope beneath the marching figures.

studyData.intro: A towering ship and sharply dressed procession turn arrival into an imposing spectacle. The image is the publisher’s 2008 edition reproduction; the picture book’s 1998 origin and documented colonisation theme are explained separately.

regions.label: An angular procession crosses the slope
regions.summary: Dark angular rabbit figures move across the pale sloping ground.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Dark angular rabbit figures move across the pale sloping ground. Their bodies, tall hats, broad brims and extended limbs overlap into a procession.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Shared direction and repeated shapes make the figures act as a group. The rhythm can feel coordinated before individual faces are examined.

regions.question: What makes these figures read as a collective arrival rather than separate characters?

regions.label: Tall hats repeat the ship’s points
regions.summary: Several dark hats rise into narrow points above pale brims.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Several dark hats rise into narrow points above pale brims. Their long angular profiles are more prominent than the small faces beneath them.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Repeating pointed hats connects the procession to the ship’s projecting geometry. The similarity can make the arrivals and their machinery feel visually related.

regions.question: How do the hats change the proportions and character of the figures?

regions.label: Pale faces inside dark costumes
regions.summary: Small pale faces and curved snouts appear among the dark clothing.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Small pale faces and curved snouts appear among the dark clothing. Their rounded contours contrast with the long straight edges around them.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The lighter faces remain discoverable inside the dense procession. Their scale also makes individual identity less immediately dominant than the group’s overall silhouette.

regions.question: Which face do you find first, and what makes it separate from the clothing?

regions.label: A vast projecting ship form
regions.summary: A huge pale ship hull or bow projects across the upper left, with small square openings and a circular emblem.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A huge pale ship hull or bow projects across the upper left, with small square openings and a circular emblem. Its long point narrows towards the right.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The scale difference makes the arrival feel imposing. This is a solid ship form in the painting, not a cloth sail; its small openings reinforce that reading.

regions.question: How do the small square openings help establish the ship’s enormous apparent size?

regions.label: A patterned red form below the hull
regions.summary: A red patterned banner-like form curves below the pale hull beside a dark pointed edge.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A red patterned banner-like form curves below the pale hull beside a dark pointed edge. Small yellow marks give its red surface internal detail.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The warm accent links the ship area to the red elements among the figures. Its curve also interrupts the otherwise long, pointed construction.

regions.question: What does this curved red form contribute to the surrounding sharp geometry?

regions.label: A slope reinforced by dark marks
regions.summary: The pale ground tilts across the lower cover.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The pale ground tilts across the lower cover. Long dark strokes extend in a related direction beneath and around the marching figures.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The ground marks reinforce movement already present in the procession. They can make the whole lower field seem directional rather than merely supporting the feet.

regions.question: Would the march feel as forceful on a level, unmarked ground?

regions.label: Yellow clouds surround a dark opening
regions.summary: Yellow cloud masses gather on the right around a deep dark sky opening.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Yellow cloud masses gather on the right around a deep dark sky opening. Their soft painted transitions differ from the hard-edged hats and hull.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The softer forms create contrast with the arriving construction. The dark opening also provides a quieter place for the white title.

regions.question: How does the cloud edge affect your reading of the sharply pointed ship?

regions.label: White words in the dark sky
regions.summary: The Rabbits sits in pale lettering within the dark upper opening.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The Rabbits sits in pale lettering within the dark upper opening. Its modest size leaves the large painted forms dominant.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The title is easy to locate because the surrounding sky is comparatively quiet. It need not be large to establish a clear verbal point of entry.

sections.heading: A simple name for a strange arrival
sections.body: The title identifies rabbits in plain English, while the pictured figures and their machinery are highly stylised. The contrast between familiar naming and unfamiliar appearance is visible on this cover.

regions.question: What makes this small title legible amid such a dramatic image?

regions.label: Two names share the line
regions.summary: John Marsden and Shaun Tan are named beneath the title in a small pale line.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: John Marsden and Shaun Tan are named beneath the title in a small pale line. Their names share the same dark area rather than separate image panels.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The shared line presents a collaborative work. Its smaller scale keeps the title first while still making the makers discoverable in the same glance.

sections.heading: A deliberately unsettling fable
sections.body: Marsden wrote the text and Tan made the images. Tan describes the book as a fable about colonisation told from the viewpoint of the colonised. That documented context supports discussing power and arrival here, without treating the strange pictured ship as a literal historical vessel.

regions.question: What do the two names invite you to ask about how words and pictures were made?

regions.label: A gold circle belongs to the edition
regions.summary: A gold circular medallion sits near the lower right edge.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A gold circular medallion sits near the lower right edge. Its rim lettering and central device differ from the painted scene’s irregular forms.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The medallion adds a publishing signal to the image. The circle is easy to distinguish from the sloping ground and angular figures around it.

sections.heading: The edition and the original work
sections.body: Hachette lists this Lothian hardback, ISBN 9780734410788, as published on 1 May 2008. The original picture book dates from 1998. The current publisher image, including its medallion, is tied to the selected edition rather than presented as an untouched first-cover scan.

regions.question: How does a medal-like device change your expectations before you open a book?

connections.label: An angular arrival
connections.title: Hats and ship points
connections.text: Pointed hats echo the large ship’s projecting point, giving the arrival a coordinated rhythm.
